name: Distribution Is Part of the Product

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether the company has an economically viable route from product to customers, revenue, talent, and capital.
positioning.productLabel: Distribution Lens — based on Peter Thiel's public teaching and CS183 materials
notAClaimOf: proof that sales matters more than product

attribution.display: Based on Peter Thiel public distribution teaching with Blake Masters CS183 notes

neutralParaphrase: A product does not become a business merely by being technically strong. The company needs a repeatable distribution motion compatible with customer value, contract size, sales cycle, retention, gross margin, and cash consumption. Simplified CLV/CAC relations are starting constraints, not a complete underwriting model.

locator.value: Sections I, II, IV, and V
Page-level locator pending authorized PDF review

requiredConditions: The company has a defined customer or stakeholder whose adoption is necessary.
The purchasing, adoption, or viral mechanism can be described.
Available data are normalized to the company's business model and stage.

requiredEvidence.description: Named channel, buyer, user, decision process, and repeatable acquisition steps.
Gross-margin-adjusted customer value, acquisition cost, payback, retention, and expansion using explicit definitions.
Sales cycle, conversion, pipeline quality, rep ramp, channel cost, or viral coefficient appropriate to the model.
Evidence showing whether acquisition economics and implementation burden hold as volume or segment expands.

decisionQuestions: Who buys, who uses, who approves, and who can block adoption?
Which distribution motion fits the contract value and sales complexity?
Are customer value and acquisition cost calculated from compatible cohorts and definitions?
How long does cash remain tied up before gross-margin contribution recovers acquisition cost?
Does implementation, support, or custom work grow with revenue?
What channel or sales evidence proves repeatability beyond founder-led selling?
What distribution mechanism is difficult for a competitor to copy?
positiveSignals: The buyer, user, champion, and procurement path are explicit.
Cohort economics include gross margin, retention, payback, and service burden.
A channel repeatedly converts similar customers without founder dependence.
Sales efficiency remains stable or improves across cohorts and segments.
Distribution creates proprietary access, data, workflow, or referral effects.
The company names conditions under which the channel becomes uneconomic.
redFlags: The plan assumes the product will sell itself.
CLV uses revenue without gross margin or realistic retention.
CAC excludes sales labor, implementation, incentives, or failed acquisition.
Founder-led sales are projected as a mature repeatable channel.
Pipeline is treated as contracted revenue.
Growth requires increasing custom work or subsidies.
A complex product relies on low-touch distribution without adoption evidence.
disconfirmingEvidence: Newer cohorts have longer payback, lower retention, or weaker expansion.
Rep-added growth does not exceed added sales cost.
Pilot-to-paid or POC-to-production conversion is low.
Customers require implementation effort that destroys contribution margin.
The main channel changes terms, loses access, or becomes saturated.
Referrals do not persist without incentives.
contraindications: Do not use the simplified course CLV formula as the runtime calculation.
Do not compare distribution metrics across incompatible business models without normalization.
Do not interpret missing mature metrics as automatic failure at pre-seed; instead request stage-appropriate experiments.

instructions: Map buyer, user, blocker, channel, sales motion, and adoption steps.
Use deterministic specialist calculations for unit economics.
Evaluate repeatability, scalability, and defensibility from source-backed cohorts.
Separate current evidence from future distribution plans.
Return the most decision-changing missing distribution evidence.

deterministicRule.reason: The specialist engine owns deterministic metrics; this card interprets their evidence and fit.

sourceReliability.low: Only an uncited distribution summary is available.
sourceReliability.medium: Course notes support the doctrine but direct transcript pages are not reviewed.
sourceReliability.high: Authorized Peter Thiel transcript pages and derivative-note locators are both reviewed.

evidenceStrength.low: Planned channel and founder anecdotes only.
evidenceStrength.medium: One repeatable cohort or channel with partial economics.
evidenceStrength.high: Multiple source-backed cohorts show repeatability, attractive economics, and stable implementation burden.

evidenceCoverage.low: Buyer, channel, economics, or retention is missing.
evidenceCoverage.medium: All required fields exist but scalability or service burden is incomplete.
evidenceCoverage.high: Motion, economics, cohorts, scalability, and counterevidence are documented.

applicabilityConfidence.low: No commercial adoption path is relevant yet.
applicabilityConfidence.medium: A path exists but stage limits measurable repeatability.
applicabilityConfidence.high: Distribution is a central, observable constraint on company outcomes.

judgmentConfidence.low: Only channel plausibility can be assessed.
judgmentConfidence.medium: Initial repeatability exists but economics or scaling is unresolved.
judgmentConfidence.high: Channel, cohorts, economics, and scaling behavior converge.

promotionRequirements: Complete the authorized Stanford transcript revision and page locators.
Delegate all calculations to versioned specialist formulas.
Test incremental judgment utility after unit economics are already known.
empiricalQualifications: Distribution metrics are stage- and model-dependent.
Founder-led sales can validate demand without yet proving scale.
CLV estimates are highly sensitive to retention and margin assumptions.

rights.notes: No course worksheet or long passage is reproduced.

openIssues: Hash and review the Stanford PDF source revision.
